title: Reading Data: Tables, Charts and Averages
summary: Learn to read tables and charts, spot misleading graphs, calculate averages and percentages, and question claims that use numbers.
audience: Students from secondary school upwards who want to read and question numbers in school, news and work

body.p: A table is the simplest way to show data. Before you look at any number, read three things: the title (what is being measured), the headings of the rows and columns (what each line and column means), and the units (marks, naira, cedis, kilograms, per cent). Many mistakes come from skipping this step. A column headed 'Population' could mean thousands of people or millions, and the table must tell you which.
Here is a made-up survey that we will use through the whole course. A class of 30 students was asked how they usually travel to school. Each student gave one answer.

body.code:
How students travel to school (class of 30)

Method      Students
Walk              12
Bus                9
Bicycle            3
Car                6
Total             30

body.h: Reading across, down and the total

list: Read down a column to compare values of the same kind, for example the number of students for each method.
Read across a row to see everything about one item, for example Bus: 9 students.
Always check the total. Here 12 + 9 + 3 + 6 = 30, which matches the class size, so every student is counted once.
If a total does not match what you expect, look for missing rows, double counting or a different unit.

body.p: A count on its own is hard to judge, so turn it into a fraction or a percentage of the total. Walking is 12 out of 30, which is 12 divided by 30 = 0.4, or 40%. Bicycle is 3 out of 30 = 0.1, or 10%. Now you can say clearly that four in every ten students walk, and only one in ten cycles.

body.h: Questions to ask of any table

steps: Read the title and the units. What exactly was counted or measured, and when?
Check who or what is in the table. All 30 students, or only some?
Find the largest and smallest values and say what they are in a full sentence.
Compare using fractions or percentages, not only raw counts, especially when groups are different sizes.
Check the source and the date at the bottom. Old data may no longer describe today.

body.tip: When two groups have different sizes, never compare raw counts. A school in Lagos with 120 absent students out of 2,400 and a school in Banjul with 40 absent out of 400 have very different absence rates, even though 120 and 40 look like a fair comparison. Divide first: 120 / 2400 = 5% and 40 / 400 = 10%.

lessons.title: Bar charts, line charts and pie charts

body.p: A chart turns a table into a picture so that patterns are quicker to see. Each type of chart suits a different job. Choosing the wrong one makes a chart hard to read, and reading a chart wrongly leads to wrong conclusions. Start with the title, the labels on each axis and the units, just as you do for a table.

In a bar chart each bar stands for one category and its length shows the value. Our travel-to-school data fits well: the bar for Walk reaches 12, Bus 9, Car 6 and Bicycle 3. You can see at a glance that Walk is the longest bar and Bicycle the shortest. Bars should start at zero so that the length is fairly proportional to the value.

body.h: Line charts show change over time

body.p: A line chart joins points that are measured in order, usually over time. Imagine a shop that records its sales each day in a week (example numbers): Monday 20, Tuesday 25, Wednesday 22, Thursday 30, Friday 40. The line rises overall, with a small dip on Wednesday. Read the shape: a steep climb means fast growth, a flat line means little change, and a fall means a decrease. Only use a line chart when the order along the bottom matters.

body.h: Pie charts show parts of a whole

body.p: A pie chart splits one whole into slices. The whole circle is 360 degrees and also represents 100%. To draw a slice, multiply its share by 360. For our survey: Walk is 40% of 360 = 144 degrees, Bus is 9/30 = 30% so 108 degrees, Bicycle is 10% so 36 degrees and Car is 20% so 72 degrees. Check: 144 + 108 + 36 + 72 = 360, so the slices fill the circle exactly.

list: Use a bar chart to compare separate categories.
Use a line chart to follow a quantity through time.
Use a pie chart only when you have a few slices that add up to a meaningful whole. With many slices, a bar chart is easier to read.
If the slices or percentages in a pie chart do not add up to 100%, something is wrong.

body.tip: When you see a chart on your phone, zoom in and read the axis numbers and the small print. A chart that looks dramatic at thumbnail size may show a very small change once you read the numbers.

body.p: Charts are persuasive, and that is why some people use them to push an opinion rather than to explain the facts. You do not need to assume anyone is lying. Many misleading charts are simply careless. Learning the common tricks lets you spot them quickly.

Imagine two bars showing the pass rate of two schools: School A scores 96 and School B scores 100. If the vertical axis starts at 0, the bars look almost the same, which is honest because 100 is only about 4.2% more than 96 (4 divided by 96). Now suppose the axis starts at 90. The bar for A is drawn 96 - 90 = 6 units tall and B is 100 - 90 = 10 units tall. B now looks 10 / 6, about 1.67 times as tall, so it appears nearly 70% bigger. The numbers did not change, only the starting point of the axis.

A line chart of rainfall, prices or exam results can show only the months that support a story. A chart showing three rising months can hide that the previous year was higher. Always ask: why does the chart start and stop where it does? What happened before and after?

list: Axes with uneven steps, such as 0, 10, 20, 50, 100 spaced equally.
Two vertical axes with different scales, arranged so that two lines appear to match.
Three-dimensional bars or pies, where the front slice looks larger than it really is.
Pictures of different sizes used as bars, where doubling the height also doubles the width so the area looks four times larger.
Missing labels, missing units or no source.

body.tip: A quick test is to ask what the chart would look like if the axis started at zero and covered a longer period. If the story disappears, the chart was exaggerating.

body.p: An average is a single number that tries to describe the middle or typical value of a data set. There are three common averages, and each answers a slightly different question. The range tells you how spread out the values are. Use the marks of nine students in a test (out of 100): 45, 52, 60, 60, 63, 68, 72, 75, 90.
The mean is the total divided by how many values there are. The total is 45 + 52 + 60 + 60 + 63 + 68 + 72 + 75 + 90 = 585. There are 9 marks, so the mean is 585 / 9 = 65.

The median is the middle value when the data are in order. Our nine marks are already in order, and the fifth one is the middle, so the median is 63. With an even number of values there are two middle ones and the median is halfway between them. For 8, 10, 12 and 20 the middle pair is 10 and 12, so the median is 11 (the mean is 12.5, different because of the big value 20).

The mode is the value that appears most often. In our marks 60 appears twice and every other mark once, so the mode is 60. A set can have more than one mode or none. The range is the highest value minus the lowest: 90 - 45 = 45. A small range means the values are close together.

The mean uses every value, so one extreme value can drag it a long way. Suppose five workers in a small firm earn 80,000, 90,000, 95,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000 naira a month (made-up numbers). The total is 1,365,000, so the mean is 273,000. Yet four of the five earn 100,000 or less. The median is 95,000, which describes a typical worker much better. When there are extreme values, the median is usually more honest. The mode is best for categories, such as the most common shoe size to stock in a shop.

list: Mean: add up and divide. Good for fairly even data.
Median: put in order and take the middle. Good when extreme values exist.
Mode: most frequent. Good for categories and counting.
Range: highest minus lowest. Shows spread.

body.tip: When a headline says 'the average', ask which average. Politicians and advertisers can choose the one that looks best.

body.p: Per cent means 'out of 100'. A percentage lets you compare quantities of different sizes on the same scale. To find a percentage of an amount, change the percentage to a decimal and multiply. 25% of 8 is 0.25 x 8 = 2. A shop in Nairobi sells a bag for 1,200 shillings and takes 25% off. The discount is 0.25 x 1,200 = 300 shillings, so you pay 1,200 - 300 = 900 shillings.

To measure how much something has grown or shrunk, use this formula: change divided by the original value, times 100. The original is always the starting value. If the price of a loaf goes from 250 to 300, the change is 300 - 250 = 50, and 50 / 250 = 0.2, so the price rose by 20%. A common error is dividing by the new value: 50 / 300 is about 16.7%, which is wrong.

body.code:
Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100

250 -> 300 : (300 - 250) / 250 x 100 = 20% increase
300 -> 250 : (250 - 300) / 300 x 100 = about 16.7% decrease

body.p: Notice that going back down is a different percentage. If a price rises from 200 to 250, that is a 25% increase. If it falls from 250 to 200, that is a 20% decrease, because now the original is 250. Likewise, a price of 100 that rises 20% becomes 120, and then falls by 20% to 96. It does not return to 100, because the second 20% is taken from a larger number.

When one percentage changes to another, say which kind of change you mean. If 30% of students in a school own a laptop one year and 36% the next, the rise is 6 percentage points (36 - 30). The relative rise is 6 / 30 = 20%. Both statements are true, but they sound very different, so a careful writer says which one.

steps: Write down the old (starting) value and the new value.
Subtract: new minus old. A negative answer means a decrease.
Multiply by 100 and add the % sign.
Say whether it is a rise or fall, and what the start was.

body.tip: A score of 40 out of 50 is 40 / 50 x 100 = 80%. Always check that the numbers you divide are the part and the whole, in that order.

lessons.title: Correlation, samples, bias and good questions

body.p: The last skill is judging claims. Numbers can be correct and the conclusion still wrong. Three ideas protect you: correlation is not causation, samples must be fair, and every claim deserves questions.

Two things are correlated when they tend to rise and fall together. It does not follow that one causes the other. Ice-cream sales and the number of people swimming both rise in hot months. Ice cream does not cause swimming; hot weather is a hidden third factor that drives both. Sometimes the link is just chance, and sometimes the cause runs the other way. To show cause, you need more evidence, such as a fair experiment that compares a group that receives a treatment with a similar group that does not.

We rarely ask everyone, so we ask a sample and hope it represents the whole group. A good sample is large enough and chosen in a way that gives everyone a fair chance. A bad sample is biased. If you want to know how many hours students study, and you ask only students you find in the library, you will overestimate, because library users study more than most. A phone poll reaches only people with phones who answer calls. Even a large sample can be biased if it is chosen badly, while a smaller fair sample is often more useful. Be careful with small groups too: if 15 of 20 students prefer a revision method, that is 75%, but 20 students tell you little about a whole country.

list: Who was asked, and how were they chosen?
How many were asked? A sample of 50 out of 1,000 students is 5% of the school, so check that those 50 are typical.
Were the questions worded fairly, or did they lead people to an answer?
Who paid for the research and what do they want you to believe?

body.h: Asking good questions of a claim

body.p: Suppose an advert says 'Our course cuts exam failure by 50%'. Ask: 50% of what? If failure went from 4 students to 2, that is a 50% fall, but only two students. Compared with whom, and over what period? Who measured it? Is anything missing, such as a comparison group? These questions work on news, social media and school reports.

body.tip: Before you share a statistic, read the whole article, check the source and look for the numbers behind the percentage. A single surprising number is more often a mistake or an exaggeration than a discovery.

quiz.q: In the travel survey of 30 students, 3 cycle to school. What share of the class cycles?
A pie chart slice represents 25% of a total. How many degrees is the slice?
A teacher wants to show how a school's attendance changed week by week over a term. Which chart suits this best?
options: A line chart, because the weeks are in order
A pie chart, because attendance is a percentage
A bar chart with the bars in random order

quiz.q: Two bars show scores of 96 and 100, drawn on an axis that starts at 90. About how many times as tall does the second bar look?
A chart shows a company's profit rising for three months and the caption says 'Profits are soaring'. What should you check first?
options: Whether the chart has a colourful design
Whether the company has a large office
How many people liked the chart
What the figures were before those three months

quiz.q: The test scores 70, 65, 80 and 85 have what mean?
Five salaries include one very large value that is far above the others. Which average describes a typical salary best?
What is the median of 3, 5, 9 and 13?
A shop owner records shoe sizes sold: 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8. Which statistic tells her the size to stock most of?
The highest mark in a class is 88 and the lowest is 31. What is the range?
A school has 4,500 students and 20% of them walk to school. How many walk?
A price rises from 80 to 100. What is the percentage increase?
In one year 40% of households in a town have internet, and the next year 46% do. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 6%, and that is the only correct way to say it
It rose by 6 percentage points, which is a 15% relative increase
It rose by 6 percentage points, which is a 6% relative increase

quiz.q: Data show that towns with more umbrellas sold also have more traffic jams. What is the best conclusion?
options: The two are correlated, but a third factor such as rain might explain both
Traffic jams cause umbrellas to be sold

quiz.q: A survey about how much students study asks only people sitting in the library. What is the main problem?
options: The sample is too fair to be trusted
The mean cannot be calculated from library data
The sample is biased because library users probably study more than average

quiz.q: An advert says 'Our app cuts mistakes by 50%'. Which question is most useful to ask first?
options: 50% of what, compared with whom, and how many people were tested?
Is the advert on a popular website?
Does the app have a short name?
